title: CSC3710 2026-08-25 — What a DFA Is and a Set-Theory Refresher

questions.q: In the formal definition M = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F), what is δ?
choices: A function Q × Σ → Q giving exactly one next state for each (state, symbol) pair
A relation that may give zero or several next states for a (state, symbol) pair
The set of final states
A function Σ → Q mapping each symbol to a state
questions.explain: δ is the **transition function** with domain Q × Σ. Because it is a *function* on all of Q × Σ, every (state, symbol) pair has exactly one next state — that is the formal meaning of *deterministic*. Zero-or-many next states describes an NFA.

questions.q: Which statement about F, the set of final states, is correct?
choices: F ⊆ Q, and F may be empty, contain some states, or contain all of them
F must contain exactly one state
F must be nonempty, otherwise the machine is not a DFA
F must not contain the initial state q₀
questions.explain: F is any subset of Q, including ∅ and Q itself. The monster FSM having no final states is therefore *not* a problem. q₀ may be final (it just means the empty string is accepted) — the vending machine avoids it for modelling reasons, not because the definition forbids it.

questions.q: Which of these must be specified for a machine to be a DFA in this course's sense?
choices: A finite set of states
Exactly one initial state
An explicit alphabet
A set of final states (possibly empty)
A transition for every (state, symbol) pair
At least one final state
questions.explain: The five components are Q, Σ, δ (total), q₀ and F. F must be *specified* but may be ∅, so "at least one final state" is not required.

questions.q: A DFA may have two initial states as long as they have the same outgoing transitions.
questions.explain: The definition has a single q₀ ∈ Q. Processing must start at one well-defined state; two start states would make the computation ambiguous (that kind of freedom belongs to nondeterministic models).

questions.q: What exactly makes a finite automaton *deterministic*?
choices: From every state there is exactly one outgoing transition for each symbol of the alphabet
It has exactly one final state
Every state has at most one outgoing transition
It never contains self-loops
questions.explain: Determinism = for every state q and symbol a there is exactly one arrow labelled a out of q. Self-loops are fine (δ(q, a) = q), and the number of final states is irrelevant. "At most one" allows missing transitions, which makes the machine partial.

questions.q: In the formal definition, the alphabet Σ must be a finite, nonempty set.
questions.explain: Σ is a finite nonempty set of symbols, e.g. {Q, H} for the vending machine. Q is also finite — that finiteness is the "finite" in DFA.

questions.q: For the vending machine, which is the correct value of δ(25¢, H)?
questions.explain: From 25¢, inserting a half dollar adds 50¢, giving 75¢. (δ(25¢, Q) = 50¢.)

questions.q: Why is the vending machine's initial state 0¢ **not** a final state?
choices: If it were final, the empty input would be accepted — a free bottle at power-on
The definition forbids the initial state from being final
A DFA may only have one final state and 100¢+ is already final
Final states must have self-loops
questions.explain: Acceptance checks the state after the last symbol. With no coins the machine stays at 0¢, so making 0¢ final would accept ε, i.e. release water before any money is inserted. The definition itself would allow it; the model's meaning does not.

questions.q: A DFA's state diagram is a directed, labelled graph in which each vertex has exactly one outgoing edge with each alphabet label.
questions.explain: Vertices = states, edges = transitions (q, a, δ(q, a)), labels = symbols. "Exactly one outgoing edge per label from every vertex" is the graph form of determinism.

questions.q: The vending machine has 5 states and alphabet {Q, H}. How many transitions does it have as a complete DFA?
questions.explain: |Q| · |Σ| = 5 × 2 = 10 — one per cell of the transition table. JFLAP draws only 9 arrows because the two 75¢ → 100¢+ transitions share one arrow with stacked labels.

questions.q: A complete DFA has 7 states over the alphabet {a, b, c}. How many transitions does it have?
questions.explain: Each of the 7 states needs one transition per symbol: 7 × 3 = 21.

questions.q: A partial automaton has 7 states over {a, b, c}. It is completed by adding one trap state. How many transitions does the completed DFA have?
questions.explain: The completed machine has 8 states, so 8 × 3 = 24 transitions. The trap state contributes 3 self-loops, and every previously missing pair now points to it.

questions.q: In class the transition count was first described as "input squared". Why is that wrong in general?
choices: The count is |Q| × |Σ|; it equals |Σ|² only when the number of states happens to equal the alphabet size
The count is |Q|², since each state connects to each state
The count is |Q| + |Σ|
It is correct: a DFA always has |Σ|² transitions
questions.explain: Each state needs one arrow per symbol, so transitions = states × symbols. 5 states with 5 inputs gives 25 (= 5²) only by coincidence; 6 states with 5 inputs gives 30.

questions.q: In JFLAP, one arrow from q1 to q2 carries the stacked labels `a` and `b`. How many transitions does it represent?
choices: It depends on whether q2 is final
0 — stacked labels are invalid in a DFA
questions.explain: JFLAP merges transitions with the same source and target into one drawn arrow, but logically each symbol is a separate transition. Count labels, not arrows.

questions.q: The monster FSM has 5 states, 5 inputs, and its table lists 11 transitions. How many transitions are missing for it to be complete?
questions.explain: A complete machine needs 5 × 5 = 25 transitions; 25 − 11 = 14 are missing.

questions.q: The monster FSM (5 states, 5 inputs) is completed by adding a trap state. How many transitions does the completed machine have?
questions.explain: 6 states × 5 inputs = 30. The 14 missing pairs go to the trap state and the trap state has 5 self-loops (11 + 14 + 5 = 30).

questions.q: A DFA over {0, 1} has 12 states. How many rows × columns (cells) does its transition table have, i.e. how many transitions?
questions.explain: 12 states × 2 symbols = 24; every cell holds exactly one next state.

questions.q: The vending machine: states 0¢ (initial), 25¢, 50¢, 75¢, 100¢+ (final); Q adds 25¢, H adds 50¢, reaching ≥ 1 dollar goes to 100¢+, and 100¢+ behaves like 0¢ on the next coin. Is `H Q Q` accepted?
choices: Rejected: it ends in 75¢
Rejected: it ends in 25¢
Accepted: it passes through 50¢
questions.explain: 0¢ —H→ 50¢ —Q→ 75¢ —Q→ 100¢+. The input ends in the final state, so it is accepted.

questions.topic: Trace Q Q Q Q H
questions.q: The vending machine: states 0¢ (initial), 25¢, 50¢, 75¢, 100¢+ (final); Q adds 25¢, H adds 50¢, reaching ≥ 1 dollar goes to 100¢+, and 100¢+ behaves like 0¢ on the next coin. Is `Q Q Q Q H` accepted?
choices: Rejected: it ends in 50¢
Accepted: a bottle was released after the fourth coin
Accepted: it ends in 100¢+
Rejected: it ends in 0¢
questions.explain: 0¢ → 25¢ → 50¢ → 75¢ → 100¢+ (bottle) —H→ 50¢. Acceptance only looks at the state after the **last** symbol, which is 50¢, so it is rejected even though a bottle was released mid-input.

questions.q: The vending machine: states 0¢ (initial), 25¢, 50¢, 75¢, 100¢+ (final); Q adds 25¢, H adds 50¢, reaching ≥ 1 dollar goes to 100¢+, and 100¢+ behaves like 0¢ on the next coin. Which state is the machine in after reading `Q Q H Q`?
questions.explain: 0¢ —Q→ 25¢ —Q→ 50¢ —H→ 100¢+ —Q→ 25¢. The coin after a purchase starts a new count, so one quarter puts it at 25¢.

questions.q: The vending machine: states 0¢ (initial), 25¢, 50¢, 75¢, 100¢+ (final); Q adds 25¢, H adds 50¢, reaching ≥ 1 dollar goes to 100¢+, and 100¢+ behaves like 0¢ on the next coin. The input `Q Q Q H` is accepted.
questions.explain: 0¢ → 25¢ → 50¢ → 75¢ —H→ 100¢+. From 75¢ a half dollar gives 1.25 dollars; there is no change, but the total reaches ≥ 1 dollar so the machine is in the final state.

questions.q: The vending machine: states 0¢ (initial), 25¢, 50¢, 75¢, 100¢+ (final); Q adds 25¢, H adds 50¢, reaching ≥ 1 dollar goes to 100¢+, and 100¢+ behaves like 0¢ on the next coin. The empty string is accepted.
questions.explain: With no input the machine stays in q₀ = 0¢, which is not final, so ε is rejected — precisely why 0¢ was not made final.

questions.q: The vending machine: states 0¢ (initial), 25¢, 50¢, 75¢, 100¢+ (final); Q adds 25¢, H adds 50¢, reaching ≥ 1 dollar goes to 100¢+, and 100¢+ behaves like 0¢ on the next coin. Which inputs are accepted?
choices: `H H`
`H H H`
`Q H Q H`
`H Q Q H H`
`Q H H`

questions.q: Which best describes L(vending machine)?
choices: All coin sequences whose last coin completes a purchase
All coin sequences totalling at least 1 dollar
All coin sequences that release at least one bottle
All coin sequences of length at least 2
questions.explain: A string is accepted iff the machine ends in 100¢+. `H H Q` totals 1.25 dollars and releases a bottle, but ends in 25¢ and is rejected — so only the last-coin description is right.

questions.q: How does the vending machine model "the next coin starts a new count" without an ε-move back to 0¢?
choices: 100¢+ is given the same outgoing transitions as 0¢ (Q → 25¢, H → 50¢)
100¢+ has self-loops on Q and H
100¢+ has a transition to 0¢ that consumes no input
The machine halts in 100¢+
questions.explain: A DFA never moves without consuming a symbol, so it can't "reset" for free. Copying 0¢'s transitions onto 100¢+ gives the same future behaviour, and the machine never needs to revisit 0¢.

questions.q: In a DFA, every transition consumes exactly one input symbol.
questions.explain: The machine reads left to right and follows δ once per symbol; it never moves without input. (ε/λ-moves appear only in nondeterministic models.)

questions.q: Which of the following is a **language** over Σ = {0, 1}?
choices: {0, 1} viewed as the set of symbols
The string 0110
δ(q₀, 0)
questions.explain: A language is any set of strings over Σ, i.e. a subset of Σ\*. {0, 1} as a set of symbols is the alphabet; 0110 is a single string.

questions.q: If the English **words** are taken as the alphabet, what plays the role of the language?
choices: The set of valid English sentences
The set of letters a–z
The set of all English words
A single sentence such as "I like dogs"
questions.explain: Symbols = words, strings = sequences of words (sentences), language = the set of valid sentences. "I like dogs" is in it; "dogs like I" is not.

questions.q: As strings, `ab` and `ba` are equal because they contain the same symbols.
questions.explain: A string is a **sequence** of symbols, and sequences care about order, so `ab` ≠ `ba` — unlike the sets {a, b} = {b, a}.

questions.q: For every string w, what are εw and wε?
choices: Both equal w
Both equal ε
εw = w but wε is undefined
Both equal ∅
questions.explain: ε is the identity for concatenation, just as 0 is for addition and 1 for multiplication. JFLAP writes it λ.

questions.q: What is the length |w| of the string w = `QHQH` over {Q, H}?
questions.explain: The length is the number of symbols in the sequence: 4.

questions.q: Σ\* contains the empty string.
questions.explain: Σ\* is the set of all finite strings over Σ, including the one of length 0.

questions.q: JFLAP writes λ where Sipser writes ε. What do they denote?
choices: The same thing: the empty string, of length 0
λ is the empty set, ε is the empty string
λ is a special alphabet symbol
ε is a transition, λ is a state
questions.explain: Both are notations for the empty string; which one appears depends on the book (Linz, Sudkamp and JFLAP use λ).

questions.q: Which are valid reasons the *Game Programming Gems* monster FSM is **not** a DFA under this course's definition?
choices: It has no initial state
Only 11 of the required 25 transitions are given
Its diagram shows 10 transitions while its table lists 11
It has no final states
It contains a self-loop
questions.explain: No q₀, an incomplete δ, and an inconsistent diagram/table are all real problems. F = ∅ is allowed, and self-loops are ordinary transitions.

questions.q: Game code often treats a missing (state, event) entry as "ignore the event". How is that made explicit in a complete DFA?
choices: Add δ(q, a) = q for each missing pair
Send each missing pair to a new trap state
Delete the event from the alphabet
Make q a final state
questions.explain: "Ignore and stay" is an implicit self-loop; completing it means writing δ(q, a) = q explicitly. For the monster that is 14 self-loops plus choosing an initial state (Uncaring is natural).

questions.q: When should you complete a partial automaton with a trap (dead) state rather than with self-loops?
choices: When a missing transition means "halt and reject", so the language must be preserved
When a missing transition means "ignore the input"
When the machine has no final states
Never — trap states make a machine nondeterministic
questions.explain: A trap state is non-final and loops to itself on every symbol, so once entered the string can never be accepted — exactly the partial-DFA semantics of rejecting on an undefined move. Self-loops instead change the language to "ignore the symbol".

questions.q: Which properties does a trap (dead) state have?
choices: It is not final
It has a self-loop on every alphabet symbol
It is the initial state
It has no outgoing transitions
questions.explain: It must still have one transition per symbol (determinism), all pointing back to itself, and it must be non-final so nothing that enters it is accepted. "No outgoing transitions" would make the machine partial again.

questions.q: Completing a partial automaton with a trap state accepts exactly the same strings as the partial machine (which rejects on an undefined move).
questions.explain: Any string that hit an undefined move now falls into the trap and ends in a non-final state — rejected either way. All other strings follow the same path as before.

questions.q: According to the Gems chapter, why describe the monster's behaviour with a state diagram rather than prose?
choices: It is a concise and unambiguous description
It is the only form a compiler can read
Diagrams automatically make the machine deterministic
Prose cannot describe self-loops
questions.explain: A diagram (or table) gives a precise, compact specification of how the attitude changes — one reason these machines are worth studying. The chapter's own inconsistencies show that the precision only helps if you follow the definition.

questions.q: Some authors allow a *partial* transition function, but this course requires every transition to be explicit.
questions.explain: Definitions vary between books; this course requires δ to be total so the machine is well-defined.

questions.q: What is the order of machine models in the course?
choices: DFA → NFA → pushdown automaton → Turing machine
NFA → DFA → Turing machine → pushdown automaton
Turing machine → pushdown automaton → NFA → DFA
DFA → pushdown automaton → NFA → Turing machine
questions.explain: The course builds up from the simplest model; you can't start with Turing machines.

questions.q: NFAs recognize strictly more languages than DFAs.
questions.explain: Every NFA converts to an equivalent DFA (subset construction). Both recognize exactly the regular languages; NFAs are studied because they are often much easier to design.

questions.q: What does a pushdown automaton add to a finite automaton, and what does that buy?
choices: A stack; it can recognize context-free languages such as { aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0 }
A read-write tape; it can compute anything computable
Nondeterminism only; it recognizes the same languages
A second start state
questions.explain: Finite control + stack gives the context-free languages, which include non-regular ones like aⁿbⁿ (a DFA can't count unboundedly).

questions.q: Which describes a Turing machine?
choices: A finite-state control plus an unbounded tape it can read and write, with a moving head
A finite automaton with a stack
A DFA with several initial states
A DFA whose alphabet is infinite
questions.explain: The tape is readable **and writable** and unbounded. By the Church–Turing thesis, anything computable by an algorithm is computable by a Turing machine.

questions.q: An NFA has n states. Up to how many states can the equivalent DFA from the subset construction have?
choices: 2ⁿ
n²
n
2n
questions.explain: The DFA's states are *subsets* of the NFA's states, i.e. elements of the power set, and |P(S)| = 2^|S|.

questions.q: Which chain of inclusions is correct?
choices: regular ⊂ context-free ⊂ recursively enumerable
context-free ⊂ regular ⊂ recursively enumerable
recursively enumerable ⊂ context-free ⊂ regular
regular = context-free ⊂ recursively enumerable
questions.explain: DFAs/NFAs: regular; PDAs: context-free; Turing machines: recursively enumerable. Each inclusion is proper (e.g. aⁿbⁿ is context-free but not regular).

questions.q: A student says: "The set of all Java programs is finite, because every program is finite." What's the correct response?
choices: Each program is finite, but lengths are unbounded, so the set is countably infinite
Correct — a set of finite objects is finite
It is uncountably infinite, like ℝ
It is finite but too large to count
questions.explain: You can always add one more statement, so there's no longest program. Listing strings by length then alphabetically (shortlex) gives each program a finite position, so the set is countably infinite.

questions.q: Why must some languages be unrecognizable by any machine, even a Turing machine?
choices: There are countably many machines (finite descriptions) but uncountably many languages, P(Σ\*)
Some languages contain infinitely long strings
Turing machines cannot read the empty string
Every language is recognizable by some Turing machine
questions.explain: Machines are finite strings, so countably many; the set of all languages P(Σ\*) is uncountable (Cantor's diagonal argument). Not every language can get a machine.

questions.q: Jeffrey Ullman, co-author of a standard automata textbook, shared the 2020 Turing Award with whom?
choices: Alfred Aho
Donald Knuth
Leslie Lamport
Ron Rivest
questions.explain: Aho and Ullman won "for fundamental algorithms and theory underlying programming language implementation". Knuth won in 1974 (TeX is his; LaTeX is Lamport's), and RSA's inventors in 2002.
Open only the outer backpack: its two elements are {∅} and {∅, {∅}}. Neither *is* ∅; ∅ appears only inside them.
{∅} is literally one of the two top-level elements.
The empty set has no elements at all, so nothing — not even ∅ — belongs to it.
{∅} is a backpack holding one item, an empty backpack. That item is ∅.
The only element of {a} is a, not the set {a}. Compare {a} ∈ { {a} } (true) and a ∈ {a} (true): both have the shape x ∈ {x}.
The elements are the numbers 0, 1, 2. The *set* {1} is a different object from the number 1. (But {1} ⊆ {0, 1, 2} is true.)

questions.q: Which statements are true?
questions.explain: ∈ asks whether x is one of the items; ⊆ asks whether every item of A is in S. ∅ ⊆ anything is true, but ∅ is not an item of {1}. {1} is an item of { {1} }, but {1} ⊆ { {1} } would need 1 ∈ { {1} }, which fails.

questions.q: How many elements does X = { {∅}, {∅, {∅}} } have?
questions.explain: Count the top-level commas (one) and add one: two elements, {∅} and {∅, {∅}}. Inner backpacks count as single items.

questions.q: Which is the precise reading of { {∅}, {∅, {∅}} }?
choices: A set of two elements: a set consisting of the empty set, and a set consisting of the empty set and the set consisting of the empty set
A set of three elements: the empty set, the empty set, and the set consisting of the empty set
A set of two empty sets
The empty set nested three times
questions.explain: Reading structurally from the outside in keeps every level of braces straight.

questions.q: Which of these is a mathematical **statement** (proposition)?
choices: Nashville is the capital of Tennessee.
Is 5 prime?
Insert a quarter.
questions.explain: A statement is a declarative sentence that is true or false but not both. A question and a command aren't declarative, and x > 3 has no truth value until x is known.

questions.q: For every set S (including S = ∅), ∅ ⊆ S.
questions.explain: A ⊆ S fails only if some element of A is missing from S. ∅ has no elements, so nothing can fail — vacuously true. Written ∀S, ∅ ⊆ S.
The sets are equal (order doesn't matter), and a proper subset requires A ≠ B. {a, b} ⊆ {b, a} is true.
Sets ignore repetition, so both have exactly the elements a and b. As **multisets** they would differ.
One counterexample suffices: a ∈ {a, {b}} but a ∉ { {a}, b } (the right side contains {a}, not a).

questions.q: Let A = {a, {b}} and B = {a, b, {b}}. Which are true?
choices: A ⊆ B
A ⊂ B
B ⊆ A
A = B
questions.explain: Both a and {b} are in B, so A ⊆ B. B also has b, which A lacks, so A ≠ B and A ⊂ B. B ⊄ A because b ∉ A.

questions.q: What is enough to show A ⊄ B?
choices: One element of A that is not in B
One element of B that is not in A
Showing |A| > |B| is the only way
Showing A and B are disjoint only
questions.explain: ⊆ requires *every* element of A to be in B, so a single failing element disproves it. An element of B missing from A only shows B ⊄ A.

questions.q: Which condition is equivalent to A = B?
choices: A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A
A ⊂ B and B ⊂ A
A ∩ B ≠ ∅
questions.explain: Equal sets have exactly the same elements, i.e. each is a subset of the other. Equal cardinality isn't enough ({1} vs {2}); mutual *proper* subsets is impossible.

questions.q: Which of these are equal to their "reversed" version (e.g. X with a and b swapped)?
choices: The set {a, b}
The multiset {a, a, b}
The ordered pair (a, b) with a ≠ b
The string ab with a ≠ b
questions.explain: Sets and multisets ignore order (multisets count repetition, but still ignore order). Sequences — pairs, tuples, strings — care about order, so (a, b) ≠ (b, a) and ab ≠ ba.

questions.q: Why is a DFA written with round parentheses, (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F), rather than braces?
choices: It is a 5-tuple: the position of each component carries meaning
Braces are reserved for the empty set
Parentheses mean the components are all sets
Either is fine; it's pure style
questions.explain: Round parentheses denote a sequence, where order matters: the first entry is the state set, the second the alphabet, and so on. As a set, the components would be unordered and duplicates would collapse.

questions.q: ℕ ⊂ ℝ (proper subset).
questions.explain: Every natural number is real, and 0.5 ∈ ℝ but 0.5 ∉ ℕ, so the sets are unequal. (In this course ℕ includes 0; Sipser starts at 1.)
Every set is a subset of itself — ⊆ allows equality. It is not a *proper* subset.
∅ is missing. ∅ ⊆ S for every S, so ∅ ∈ P(S) always. With ∅ added the list has all 8 subsets.
The only subset of ∅ is ∅, so P(∅) has exactly one element. Note {∅} ≠ ∅: the power set is a backpack containing one empty backpack.

questions.q: How many elements does P(S) have if |S| = 5?
questions.explain: Each element is independently in or out of a subset: 2⁵ = 32.

questions.q: What is |P(P({x}))|?
questions.explain: P({x}) = {∅, {x}} has 2 elements, so its power set has 2² = 4: {∅, {∅}, {{x}}, {∅, {x}}}.

questions.q: What is P({∅})?
questions.explain: {∅} has one element, so it has 2¹ = 2 subsets: the empty subset ∅ and the whole set {∅}.

questions.q: For any set S, which are always elements of P(S)?
choices: S
Every element x of S
{x} for every x ∈ S
questions.explain: P(S) contains subsets, not elements: ∅, S and each singleton {x} are subsets. The element x itself is generally not a subset of S, so x ∉ P(S) in general.

questions.q: How many 2-element subsets does {a, b, c} have?
questions.explain: {a, b}, {a, c}, {b, c}. {a, b} and {b, a} are the same subset, so ordered pairs (6) overcount. Listing by size: 1 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 8.

questions.q: Why does an n-element set have 2ⁿ subsets?
choices: Each of the n elements is independently in or out: 2 · 2 · … · 2
There are n choices for each of 2 positions
Subsets come in pairs of complements
Each subset is counted twice
questions.explain: Building a subset is n independent yes/no decisions, giving 2ⁿ outcomes.
All four subsets, sizes 0, 1, 1, 2 — matches 2² = 4.

questions.q: What is |{∅}|?
questions.explain: Open the backpack: one item, an empty backpack. Don't look inside it. (|∅| = 0.)
Three top-level items, each a set; their contents don't count.
One backpack, which happens to hold three things. The outer set has a single element.
Elements: 1, 2 and {1, 2}. The repeated 1 counts once, and {1, 2} is one object distinct from 1 and 2.
The only common element is {2}; {3} ≠ {3, 4}. The intersection is { {2} }, of cardinality 1 — count the *result*, not an input set.
{1, 2} is a different object from {1} and from {2}, so the sets are disjoint and the intersection is ∅.

questions.q: What is |{ a, {a}, { {a} } }|?
questions.explain: a, {a} and { {a} } are three different objects.

questions.q: For |{ {1}, {2} } ∩ { {1}, {3} }|, a student answers 2, reasoning "there is a set containing 1 and a set containing 2". What went wrong?
choices: They counted the elements of an input set instead of the intersection, which is { {1} } with cardinality 1
Nothing; the answer is 2
They should have counted the numbers inside: 1, 2, 3
The intersection is ∅, so the answer is 0
questions.explain: First compute the intersection (elements in both sets: only {1}), then count its elements: 1.

questions.q: What does it mean for A and B to be disjoint?
choices: A ∩ B = ∅
A ∪ B = ∅
A ⊆ B
questions.explain: Disjoint sets share no elements. Then |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B|.
